lead: High boiler pressure makes steam wet by the time it reaches the turbine exhaust, and water droplets erode blades. Reheat returns the steam to the boiler after a first expansion and then expands it again. Regeneration bleeds a little steam from the turbine to warm the feedwater before it enters the boiler. Both raise the mean temperature of heat addition. Reheat mainly lifts exhaust dryness; regeneration mainly lifts efficiency. Large coal, nuclear and solar steam plants use both, and the same accounting appears in any plant with a steam turbine.
prereq: You need: how to read enthalpies and entropies from steam tables and how the four Rankine states are fixed, from Chapter 6.5.

sections.h3: Wet exhaust and the reheat fix

blocks.text: In a Rankine cycle the turbine expands steam from boiler pressure to condenser pressure. As boiler pressure rises, the expansion line on the T-s diagram moves deeper into the wet region. The last turbine stages then run on a mixture of steam and water droplets. Droplets erode blades and lower stage efficiency. Most turbines limit exhaust dryness to about 0.88-0.90; below that, blade life falls.

Reheat solves this. Steam leaves the boiler, expands in a high-pressure (HP) turbine to an intermediate pressure, and the whole flow returns to a reheater in the boiler. The reheater raises the temperature back to about the original 400-540 °C. The steam then expands in a low-pressure (LP) turbine to the condenser. On the T-s diagram this adds a second heat-addition segment at high temperature, so the mean temperature at which heat enters rises. Reheat also raises exhaust dryness. Work rises, but heat input rises too. Efficiency improves only a little; dryness improves a lot.

sections.h3: Work and heat in a reheat cycle

blocks.text: Number the states: 1 condenser exit, 2 pump exit, 3 boiler exit, 4 HP turbine exit, 5 reheater exit, 6 LP turbine exit. The plant is boiler, HP turbine, reheater, LP turbine, condenser, pump, as the figure shows.

Turbine work per kg of steam is w_t = (h3 - h4) + (h5 - h6). Here h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg. The first bracket is HP work; the second is LP work. Pump work is w_p = h2 - h1. Net work is w_net = w_t - w_p. Heat enters in two places: the boiler, q_boiler = h3 - h2, and the reheater, q_reheat = h5 - h4. Total heat input is q_in = (h3 - h2) + (h5 - h4). Cycle efficiency is η = w_net/q_in.
Do not add the reheater heat to the boiler heat twice. The boiler heats liquid from state 2 to state 3; the reheater heats steam from state 4 to state 5.

The best reheat pressure is a compromise. Too high, and the steam is still wet before reheat; too low, and the reheat heat is added at a low temperature. In large plants the best value is roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the boiler pressure. The example below uses 4 bar from 40 bar to keep the arithmetic easy; that is lower than the usual optimum.

The feedwater leaving the condenser is cold; the boiler must supply sensible heat to bring it to saturation before evaporation. Regeneration reduces that sensible heat by taking steam from the turbine and using it to warm the feedwater. The steam is called bleed steam. It expands only to the bleed point and then leaves the turbine, so it does no work below that point. Turbine work falls.

Why can efficiency rise? The boiler heat input falls more. The feedwater enters the boiler at a higher temperature, so heat addition starts at a higher temperature. The mean temperature of heat addition rises, and for the same condenser temperature the Carnot limit 1 - T<sub>reject</sub>/T<sub>mean,in</sub> rises. The work lost is the bleed fraction times the enthalpy drop the bleed steam would have produced below the bleed point. The heat saved is larger in a well-placed heater.

An open feedwater heater is a direct-contact mixing chamber. Bleed steam and feedwater mix and leave as saturated liquid at the bleed pressure. Each open heater needs a pump after it. A closed feedwater heater is a surface exchanger: feedwater flows inside tubes and bled steam condenses outside. The streams do not mix. The drain is cascaded to the next lower-pressure heater or returned to the condenser.

For one open heater, let y be the bleed fraction in kg bleed per kg boiler steam, h_b the bleed enthalpy, h_2 the feedwater enthalpy entering the heater, and h_3 the saturated liquid enthalpy leaving. The energy balance is y h_b + (1 - y) h_2 = h_3, so y = (h_3 - h_2)/(h_b - h_2). Find y before you sum work: only (1 - y) kg flows through the rest of the turbine.

examples.question: A 40 bar, 400 °C steam plant has a condenser at 0.1 bar. Steam leaves the boiler at h3 = 3213.6 kJ/kg. It expands in the HP turbine to 4 bar, where h4 = 2685.6 kJ/kg and x4 = 0.975. The whole flow is reheated at 4 bar to 400 °C, giving h5 = 3273.9 kJ/kg and s5 = 7.8985 kJ/kg·K. It expands in the LP turbine to 0.1 bar. Pump work is 4.0 kJ/kg and h2 = 195.8 kJ/kg. At 0.1 bar: h_f = 191.8 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2392.8 kJ/kg, s_f = 0.6493 kJ/kg·K, s_fg = 7.5009 kJ/kg·K. Find w_t, w_net, q_in, η and exhaust dryness x6.
steps: Without reheat the same plant has x6 = 0.816 and η = 35.3%, so reheat raises dryness by 0.15 and efficiency by 0.6 percentage points.
examples.check:
s5=7.8985; sf=0.6493; sfg=7.5009
x6=round((s5-sf)/sfg,4)
h6=round(191.8+x6*2392.8,1)
h3=3213.6; h4=2685.6; h5=3273.9; h1=191.8; h2=195.8
w_t=round((h3-h4)+(h5-h6),1)
w_p=round(h2-h1,1)
w_net=round(w_t-w_p,1)
q_in=round((h3-h2)+(h5-h4),1)
eta=round(w_net/q_in,4)
print(x6)
print(h6)
print(w_t)
print(w_p)
print(w_net)
print(q_in)
print(eta)

traps: Adding the reheater heat twice, or leaving it out: q_in has two separate terms, boiler (h3 - h2) and reheater (h5 - h4).
Giving bled steam full turbine work: bleed steam stops at the bleed point, so only (1 - y) kg continues to the condenser.
Using boiler pressure as the reheat pressure: the steam must expand first; the usual optimum is about one-fifth to one-quarter of boiler pressure.
Forgetting that an open feedwater heater needs a pump after it, and mixing up open (direct contact) with closed (surface) heaters.
Using h1 instead of h2 in the boiler heat term: the pump work raises the feedwater enthalpy before the boiler.

quiz.a: It takes the whole steam flow after the HP turbine and heats it back to a high temperature before the LP turbine.

quiz.q: Name the two common types of feedwater heater.
Why can bleeding steam raise cycle efficiency even though turbine work falls?
quiz.a: The bled steam gives up work below the bleed point, but the feedwater enters the boiler warmer, so the boiler heat input falls by more than the work lost; the mean temperature of heat addition rises.

quiz.q: Why does reheat raise exhaust dryness much more than it raises efficiency?
quiz.a: Reheat adds heat at an intermediate pressure, so it raises the mean temperature only a little. But it moves the end of expansion to a higher dryness, so the exhaust is much drier.

quiz.q: A reheat cycle has h3=3200, h4=2700, h5=3300, h6=2500, h2=200 kJ/kg, pump work 5 kJ/kg. Find w_net, q_in and η.
A plant adds one open feedwater heater with bleed fraction y=0.15. Explain why you cannot subtract 0.15 of the original turbine work.
quiz.a: The bled steam expands only to the bleed point. The work lost is y times the enthalpy drop from the bleed point to the condenser, not y times the whole turbine work. Also the remaining 0.85 kg does the rest of the expansion.

quiz.q: Why is the best reheat pressure not equal to the boiler pressure?
quiz.a: At boiler pressure there is no expansion before reheat, so the reheat adds heat at the same pressure and does not move the expansion end to a drier state. Some expansion must occur first.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern ultra-supercritical plants use double reheat and up to eight closed feedwater heaters with a deaerator. The search terms are feedwater heater train, drain cooler, heat rate, and supercritical Rankine cycle. Concentrated solar power with thermal storage uses the same reheat-regenerative steam cycle. Research on flexible operation studies how quickly these plants can ramp while keeping turbine blades dry.
